generation.exact_prompt: Use case: editorial feature hero illustration for a long-form film-history and media-economics article. Create a wide 16:9 cinematic editorial collage with one single, continuous, anatomically believable shark silhouette swimming calmly from left to right through successive layers of media history. Far left: murky 1910s newspaper halftone and torn columns, monochrome ink and sea haze. Next: coarse early-1960s shockumentary film grain, scratched celluloid, documentary frame edges. Center-left: lurid low-budget drive-in exploitation palette, hand-painted red, sickly yellow and turquoise, without resembling any real poster. Center: the machinery of a 1970s studio blockbuster—projector beams, marquee bulbs, television spot frames and widening theater screens—abstract, no recognizable copyrighted imagery. Center-right: franchise empire conveyed through repeating generic toy blister shapes, sequel numerals reduced to abstract geometry, merchandising grids and corporate shine. Far right: a small contemporary independent set with a consumer camera, cheap practical lamp, plywood, tape and an upload progress glow; raw, human scale, hopeful but not sentimental. The same shark remains visually continuous and unchanged across every layer, showing that the animal stays the same while media systems transform it. Deep Atlantic blue-black base, salt-white paper, oxidized red accents, tactile printmaking, torn-paper strata, restrained cinematic light, sophisticated magazine illustration, legible at thumbnail scale with strong central silhouette and generous quiet space near the top for HTML title overlay. No words, no letters, no logos, no brands, no movie characters, no swimmer, no beach victim, no blood, no attack, no giant open mouth, no Jaws-poster composition, no copyrighted composition. Full-bleed landscape, 16:9.
